My ethics is founded on pragmatism. As social animals, we have evolved specific moral intuitions (compassion, fairness, etc.). Evolutionary psychologists distinguish between familial altruism and reciprocal altruism. To put it simply, we implicitly trust our kin but trust needs to be built for unrelated groups to cooperate. Rights are a modern way of ensuring, as best as possible, that disparate groups of people can trust each other enough to cooperate on a grand scale. They are a product of intelligence and cultural evolution as opposed to a direct product of biological evolution. Our instincts came first, and "rights" were invented through generations and generations of trial, error, and careful thought.

So, take free speech. I think it is common sense that human beings have an innate desire to speak their mind, and being censored is almost always seen as a great indignity. If you look at tribal cultures, tribe members are almost always brutality honest about their opinions of each other. This creates trust, even between people who do not get along with each other. This means that it is easier to find terms upon which to cooperate. Two people who are completely honest with each other, and capable of listening to a person's opinion, will always find something they could agree to work on together. Even if they have to be in different rooms to do it.

So, what happens when a group of psychotics decide that they can't hear opinions that hurt their feelings, or inspire rage within their hearts? I'm sure we all know.

It makes quite a bit of sense, yes. "Rights" and the laws ensuring them are the way for us to bridge the differences between people; a way to extend our trust beyond whatever we would consider our tribe by setting the playing field we use. If we can agree how we play the game, then we can trust that the others in the community at very least have that same base level and can act accordingly.

That pertains to all sets of laws and social systems though, right? It seems that, after our generations of trial and error, that the systems that treat the most people as evenly as possible have produced the best results (even if they, in the US, have set the stage for the social nonsense currently sending us into a nosedive). But all legal codes set out to do this, in a wide variety of ways. Once you get outside the size of close-knit tribal settings it becomes impossible to know everyone on a personal level so having those legal codes enable a certain level of trust in those we don't know. I don't mean to imply that Christianity is solely responsible for legal codes. I would say that the particular laws, codes, traditions, etc. that our society lives by were influenced by, among a number of other things, Christianity. I would say that that particular influence is unique to Western nations. The thing I see Orban suggesting here is that influence is key to the unique perspective of Western nations and that many of the moves being made throughout Europe and elsewhere with this 'refugee' crisis are undermining that particular set of values, and once the bottom drops out we're in trouble.

Our cultural system is but one of countless ways that you could organize a society. It certainly isn't perfect, and has no intrinsic properties that make it 'better' than any other social order. Other social orders are influenced by their various philosophical and spiritual traditions as well, and as a result have cultural systems unique to their area of the world, however large or small that area is. I suppose the best concrete example of what I mean would be to look at the criticism that the Universal Declaration of Human Rights has received over the decades since it's inception. It has been said that the document is set in a way that Western cultural values feel at home in. The countries most often opposed to fully adopting the declaration are those who don't have that Christian influence in their history. Islamic and Asian states have long criticized the document as at least partially inapplicable to them and have made adjustments to their own understanding and adoption of the 'rules' set forth within. Our way of addressing the concept of human rights was seen and detracting from the moral codes of other cultures. It's not a matter of right or wrong, but simply a different way of approaching the idea that is strongly routed in traditions of the past.
